KEY MESSAGE 1...Subtropical Storm Josephine brings showers to far 
southeastern Massachusetts, along with dangerous marine conditions 
and gusty winds.

The coastal storm we've been monitoring this week acquired 
subtropical characteristics Wednesday afternoon and was classified 
as Subtropical Storm Josephine by the National Hurricane Center 
(NHC). The storm remains roughly 250 to 300 miles south-southeast of 
Nantucket over the warm waters of the Gulf Stream. So, what does 
this mean for southern New England? Simply put, the change in 
classification does not alter our expected impacts. As discussed 
last night, our forecast and messaging remain largely unchanged. In 
fact, the NHC anticipates Josephine will transition to a post-
tropical cyclone later today.

Dangerous to life-threatening marine conditions remain the primary 
concern, particularly across the ocean waters southeast of 
Nantucket. Gale Warnings remain in effect across the coastal waters. 
There is potential for a brief period of storm-force gusts of 50 kt 
or greater across the outer southeastern waters this morning into 
early afternoon. However, confidence in the coverage and duration of 
these stronger gusts remains too low to warrant an upgrade to Storm 
Warnings at this time.

On land, north to northeast wind gusts of 20 to 30 mph are expected 
across the interior, with 35 to 45 mph along the coastal plain, 
strongest across Cape Cod and the Islands. Beach erosion also 
remains possible along east-facing shorelines due to persistent 
northeast winds and large waves.

As of early this morning, KBOX radar returns show a shield of 
precipitation pivoting westward toward Cape Cod and the Islands. 
However, much of this precipitation is struggling to reach the 
ground due to dry air near the surface associated with high pressure 
to our north. Most of southern New England will remain dry, although 
a few light showers could extend as far west as southeastern 
Massachusetts, generally east of a New Bedford to Plymouth line. The 
greatest chances for measurable rainfall remain from Nantucket to 
Chatham through the first half of today.

Farther west, sunshine will allow temperatures to reach the middle 
60s, while persistent cloud cover across eastern portions of the 
region will keep highs in the upper 50s to lower 60s. Northeast 
winds gradually diminish from west to east this afternoon as 
Josephine tracks northeast into the North Atlantic, aided by an 
approaching northern-stream shortwave and associated trough.

KEY MESSAGE 2...Fairly cool on Friday with a very low chance of an 
early morning shower over the eastern waters. Otherwise, moderating 
temperatures and dry conditions are expected for the weekend into 
early next week.

As Josephine transitions to a post-tropical cyclone and departs into 
the North Atlantic, surface high pressure builds into southern New 
England from the west. A northerly breeze will likely persist 
Friday, although winds will be considerably lighter than the past 
few days as the pressure gradient relaxes. Despite abundant 
sunshine, northerly flow will maintain a cooler air mass, with highs 
mainly in the lower to middle 50s. An isolated shower cannot be 
ruled out over the eastern coastal waters early Friday, but 
otherwise dry conditions are expected.

Depending on how quickly winds decouple Friday night, Saturday 
morning could feature a frosty start across portions of the 
interior, with lows in the upper 20s to middle 30s. Similar 
overnight temperatures are possible Sunday morning as well.

Otherwise, high pressure promotes subsidence and generally quiet 
weather through the weekend and into early next week. Temperatures 
gradually moderate, with daytime highs returning to the lower and 
middle 60s and overnight lows increasing a few degrees each day as 
warmer air advects into the region aloft.

Looking ahead to Tuesday, guidance suggests a cold front may 
approach southern New England. However, the front will be situated 
between two strong areas of high pressure, limiting available 
moisture and potentially slowing its southward progression. High 
pressure may even suppress the front, allowing dry conditions to 
persist into Wednesday. Uncertainty remains regarding the timing and 
strength of any frontal passage, so it is still too early to provide 
much detail on associated sensible weather impacts.
